reason: Standard BP word for both "audience" (viewers/listeners) and "hearing" (legal/formal meeting). Cognate with English; no learner-safety issue. The example clearly illustrates the media sense.

example_pt: A audiência no tribunal começa às nove horas.
example_en: The hearing at the courthouse starts at nine o'clock.
reason: Standard BP legal/judicial term for a court hearing. The cognate English "audience" is a different sense but the example clearly anchors the judicial context, so no misleading translation risk. No learner-safety issues.

example_pt: O rato é um animal miúdo e rápido.
example_en: The mouse is a small and fast animal.
risk_note: In Brazil, "miúdo" is uncommon for "small"; prefer "pequeno". Also, EN "minute" (adj) is a false cognate. The noun sense "child" is EP usage.
reason: "Miúdo" meaning "small" or "child" is characteristic of EP; Brazilians strongly prefer "pequeno" for the adjective and "criança" for the noun. A learner using "miúdo" in Brazil will sound EP-influenced. The false_friend tag also signals the EN cognate risk.

example_pt: O efetivo da empresa inclui máquinas e imóveis.
example_en: The company's assets include machines and properties.
risk_note: In BP, "efetivo" as a noun can mean military/police strength or financial assets; the English gloss "assets" may not cover the military sense a learner encounters.
reason: Standard BP financial/accounting term for "assets." However, "efetivo" as a noun is polysemous: it also commonly means military/police personnel strength, and as an adjective means "effective/permanent." The English gloss "assets" is sense-specific, and a learner may encounter the military sense and be confused. The example constrains the financial sense well, but the ambiguity across senses warrants flagging.

example_pt: O lateral direito jogou muito bem na partida de ontem.
example_en: The right outfielder played very well in yesterday's match.
risk_note: In BP football/soccer, "lateral" means fullback/wingback, not outfielder (baseball). The English gloss "outfielder" may mislead learners into a wrong sport context.
reason: In BP, "lateral" is overwhelmingly used in football (soccer) for a fullback/wingback player. The annotation claims baseball/softball, but the example uses general football language ("partida"). The EN gloss "outfielder" is baseball-specific and unlikely to map cleanly to the BP sports usage a learner will encounter.

example_pt: Os miúdos brincam no parque toda tarde.
example_en: The children play in the park every afternoon.
risk_note: In BP, miúdo means scrawny/tiny (adj) or offal (noun), NOT child. "Child" is the EP sense. Use criança in Brazil.
reason: The sense "child" for miúdo is firmly EP. In Brazil, miúdo means small/scrawny or refers to animal offal/giblets. Teaching it as "child" would mislead BP learners; criança is the standard BP word.

example_pt: A simpatia dela conquistou todos os clientes da loja.
example_en: Her friendliness won over all the store's customers.
risk_note: False friend: in BP, simpatia most commonly means "friendliness/warmth", not English "sympathy" (condolence/pity).
reason: Standard, high-frequency BP word; the annotation explicitly flags it as a false friend with English 'sympathy'. The most common BP sense is friendliness/warmth, not condolence, making this a classic false cognate for English learners.

example_pt: O paço imperial fica no centro da cidade.
example_en: The imperial palace is in the city center.
reason: Valid BP word but low-frequency in modern everyday speech; used mainly in historical/formal contexts (e.g., Paço Imperial in Rio de Janeiro). No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: O conhecimento teórico é importante, mas a prática também.
example_en: Theoretical knowledge is important, but practice is too.
reason: Standard BP adjective meaning "theoretical"; cognate with English. No learner-safety issues.

example_pt: A simpatia dela conquista todos na festa.
example_en: Her friendliness wins everyone over at the party.
risk_note: False friend: in BP, simpatia most often means "friendliness/charm", not "sympathy" (compassion). For sympathy use compaixão or solidariedade.
reason: Standard BP word but a classic false cognate: the dominant sense is "friendliness/likability", not English "sympathy". The example confirms the BP-primary sense. Learner needs to know the EN cognate is misleading.

example_pt: A casca da árvore é grossa e marrom.
example_en: The bark of the tree is thick and brown.
reason: Common BP word for bark/peel/skin of natural objects; annotation clarifies the tree-bark sense. No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: Tirei a casca da laranja antes de comer.
example_en: I removed the skin from the orange before eating.
reason: Standard BP word for peel/skin/bark (outer covering of fruits, trees, etc.). The example clearly illustrates the fruit-peel sense. No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: Tirei a casca da laranja antes de comer.
example_en: I removed the peel from the orange before eating.
reason: Common BP word for the outer layer of fruits, vegetables, or tree bark. No learner-safety issue; the multiple English glosses (peel/skin/bark) are natural sense extensions of the same concept, not a misleading ambiguity.

example_pt: O teórico explicou sua nova ideia na conferência.
example_en: The theorist explained his new idea at the conference.
reason: Standard BP noun meaning "theorist"; cognate with English, no learner-safety issues. The en_all also lists the adjective sense "theoretical" but the annotated sense here is the noun, which is straightforward.

example_pt: O óleo vegetal é usado para cozinhar.
example_en: Vegetable oil is used for cooking.
reason: Standard BP adjective meaning "vegetable/relating to vegetables"; cognate with English; no learner-safety issue.

example_pt: O burro carrega as sacas de café na fazenda.
example_en: The donkey carries the coffee sacks on the farm.
reason: Animal sense (donkey) is the primary and unambiguous meaning here. The example clearly contextualizes the animal sense. The informal "fool" sense is common but not misleading in this context; no learner-safety issue.

example_pt: Não seja burro, estude para a prova!
example_en: Don't be a fool, study for the test!
reason: Common informal insult meaning "fool/stupid" in BP. Widely used and understood; no special sensitivity beyond being a mild pejorative. No false-friend, EP, or regional issues.

example_pt: As crianças adoram bala de morango.
example_en: The children love strawberry candy.
reason: In BP, 'bala' meaning 'candy' is completely standard and everyday. The polysemy with 'bullet/shot' is expected and not a learner-safety issue; context disambiguates clearly. No risk.

example_pt: A sé de São Paulo é uma catedral muito bonita.
example_en: The see of São Paulo is a very beautiful cathedral.
reason: Ecclesiastical/administrative term for a bishop's seat or cathedral headquarters. Standard in Brazilian Portuguese, especially in religious and geographical contexts (e.g., Sé de São Paulo). No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: Um bando de pássaros voou sobre o lago.
example_en: A flock of birds flew over the lake.
reason: Standard BP word for a group/flock of birds. Also used for gangs/bands of people, but the animal sense shown here is normal and unproblematic.

example_pt: O paciente descansava em seu leito no hospital.
example_en: The patient was resting in his bed at the hospital.
reason: Valid BP but low-frequency; primarily used in formal/literary or medical contexts (e.g., hospital bed). Everyday speech strongly prefers "cama". No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: Um bando de pássaros voou sobre a cidade.
example_en: A flock of birds flew over the city.
reason: Common BP word meaning flock/group; used for birds, people, or animals. No learner-safety issue. The annotation notes the general-group sense, which is also standard BP.

example_pt: A montagem do móvel levou duas horas.
example_en: The assembly of the furniture took two hours.
reason: Common BP word for assembly/putting together parts; also used in technical contexts (film editing). No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: A montagem do filme levou três meses.
example_en: The editing of the film took three months.
reason: Standard BP term for film/video editing in the audiovisual/cinema domain. The annotation disambiguates the sense clearly; no learner-safety concern.

example_pt: Esta cidade outrora foi a capital do país.
example_en: This city was formerly the capital of the country.
reason: Valid BP adverb meaning "formerly/in former times" but decidedly literary/formal and low-frequency in everyday speech. Brazilians would more naturally say "antigamente" or "antes". No safety risk; just a register note.

example_pt: Meu irmão pequenino tem três anos.
example_en: My little brother is three years old.
reason: Affectionate/diminutive form of pequeno; standard BP, commonly used in familial/informal contexts. No learner-safety issues.

example_pt: O pescador saiu cedo para trabalhar no mar.
example_en: The fisherman left early to work at sea.
reason: Everyday BP noun for a fisherman; no learner-safety issue.

example_pt: O pescador saiu cedo para pegar peixes.
example_en: The fisherman left early to catch fish.
reason: Standard BP noun meaning "fisherman." No learner-safety issues. The en_primary "fishing" is a minor annotation quirk but the example and en_all make the correct meaning (fisherman) clear.

example_pt: Os médicos buscam a cura para a doença.
example_en: The doctors are looking for the cure for the disease.
risk_note: Gender changes meaning: "a cura" (F) = cure; "o cura" (M) = parish priest/curate. The example uses the feminine sense only.
reason: Standard BP word. The feminine sense (cure) is safe and common. However, the masculine sense (curate/parish priest) is a distinct meaning triggered solely by grammatical gender, which could mislead learners if they encounter "o cura" expecting health vocabulary.

example_pt: A cabra come capim no quintal.
example_en: The goat eats grass in the yard.
risk_note: Feminine "cabra" = goat (animal). Masculine slang "cabra" = guy/fellow, common in Northeast Brazil. Context usually clarifies, but learners should know both senses.
reason: The (F) annotation targets the animal sense, which is standard and neutral. However, the en_all gloss "guy (M)" signals a second sense (informal/regional Northeast BR slang for a man) that could mislead a learner into thinking both senses are equally pan-Brazilian or interchangeable — worth a brief note.

example_pt: O general fez um planejamento tático antes da batalha.
example_en: The general made a tactical plan before the battle.
reason: Standard BP adjective, cognate with English "tactical"; no learner-safety issue. The en_all listing of "tactician" is a noun form and does not apply to this adjectival sense.

example_pt: Aquele cabra trabalha na padaria do bairro.
example_en: That guy works at the neighborhood bakery.
risk_note: Primarily Northeastern Brazilian slang for "guy/man". Outside that region it may sound odd or even offensive; use "cara" for safe pan-Brazilian informal "guy".
reason: The masculine "guy" sense of cabra is strongly associated with Northeastern Brazil (e.g., Pernambuco, Paraíba). In other Brazilian regions it is primarily the animal (female goat) or may carry negative connotations (scoundrel). Learners using it as a casual "guy" outside the Northeast risk sounding regional or confusing.

example_pt: O tático do time planejou a estratégia do jogo.
example_en: The team's tactician planned the game strategy.
reason: Standard BP noun meaning "tactician"; cognate with English; no learner-safety issues. Common in sports/strategy contexts.

example_pt: Ela não se apercebeu do erro na conta.
example_en: She didn't realize the mistake in the bill.
risk_note: In Brazil, "perceber" or "notar" is preferred; "aperceber-se" sounds EP/formal. Also false friend: not the same as English "perceive".
reason: Aperceber-se is understood in Brazil but strongly associated with EP usage. Brazilian speakers typically use "perceber" or "notar" for "to realize/notice". Additionally, it is a false friend for English learners who may map it to "perceive" directly, and the reflexive construction differs from English patterns.

example_pt: Minha irmã tem cabelo liso e preto.
example_en: My sister has straight, black hair.
reason: Standard BP adjective for straight/smooth hair. No learner-safety issue; common, everyday vocabulary.

example_pt: O cardeal celebrou a missa na catedral ontem.
example_en: The cardinal celebrated mass at the cathedral yesterday.
reason: Standard BP word for cardinal (religious sense); cognate with English, no learner-safety issue. Religious context is not itself a risk flag.

example_pt: O cura da igreja nova é muito simpático.
example_en: The curate of the new church is very friendly.
risk_note: Masculine sense: "o cura" = parish priest/curate. Feminine "a cura" = cure/healing — a different word. The (M) annotation marks this sense only.
reason: This sense (o cura, masculine) means parish priest/curate and is standard BP in religious contexts. The same lemma as feminine (a cura = cure) creates a genuine translation ambiguity that could mislead learners without the gender marker.

example_pt: As crianças jogam basquete na quadra da escola.
example_en: The children play basketball on the school court.
reason: Standard BP word for a sports court. The sports/annotation sense is everyday Brazilian usage (e.g., quadra de basquete, quadra poliesportiva). No learner-safety issues.

example_pt: Ele usou uma linguagem muito ordinária na reunião.
example_en: He used very vulgar language in the meeting.
risk_note: False friend: in BP, "ordinário" usually means vulgar/coarse, not simply "ordinary/usual". English "ordinary" = "comum" in BP.
reason: The dominant BP sense is "vulgar/coarse/rude" (as shown in the example), not "ordinary/usual" as English speakers would expect. Classic false cognate for English learners.

example_pt: Os quatro pontos cardeais são norte, sul, leste e oeste.
example_en: The four cardinal points are north, south, east, and west.
reason: Geography/navigation sense of 'cardeal' (ponto cardeal) is standard BP technical vocabulary. No learner-safety issue; the example clearly anchors the sense.

example_pt: Meu café da manhã ordinário é pão com manteiga.
example_en: My usual breakfast is bread with butter.
risk_note: False friend risk: English "ordinary" matches, but ordinário can also mean "vulgar/crude" in BP. Context usually clarifies, but learners should be aware of the negative sense.
reason: In BP, ordinário covers both "usual/customary" and "vulgar/low-class." The example targets the neutral/customary sense, which is valid standard BP. However, English speakers may under-estimate the negative sense, making this a partial false-friend / ambiguous cognate worth flagging.

example_pt: O chão de mármore é muito liso e brilhante.
example_en: The marble floor is very smooth and shiny.
reason: Common BP adjective meaning "smooth/straight" in the surface/texture sense. No learner-safety issue; the example is clear and unambiguous.

example_pt: O estudo estatístico mostra um aumento nas vendas.
example_en: The statistical study shows an increase in sales.
reason: Standard BP adjective in scientific/academic contexts; direct cognate of English "statistical"; no learner-safety issue.

example_pt: A grama do jardim está verde e bonita.
example_en: The grass in the garden is green and beautiful.
risk_note: Gender changes meaning: a grama = grass (F); o grama = gram (M). The example uses the feminine sense only.
reason: Standard BP word; the annotation #gendered-meaning signals that masculine/feminine forms carry different meanings. Learner needs to know gender determines which word they are using, or they risk confusing grass with the unit of weight.

example_pt: Muitos problemas provêm da falta de comunicação.
example_en: Many problems come from a lack of communication.
reason: Valid BP but low-frequency; formal/literary register. Everyday speech prefers "vir de" or "originar-se de". No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: O estatístico analisou os dados da pesquisa.
example_en: The statistician analyzed the survey data.
reason: Standard BP noun for a statistician; technical/scientific domain word with no learner-safety issues. Cognate with English, so no false-friend risk.

example_pt: A mesa de madeira maciça é muito pesada.
example_en: The solid wood table is very heavy.
reason: Standard BP adjective meaning "solid/massive (not hollow)"; no learner-safety issue. Example is natural and unambiguous.

example_pt: Ele é oriundo de uma família italiana.
example_en: He is from an Italian family.
reason: Valid BP adjective meaning "originating from / hailing from", but formal/literary in tone; everyday speech prefers "de" or "nascido em". No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: Preciso de duzentos gramas de queijo.
example_en: I need two hundred grams of cheese.
risk_note: Gender changes meaning: "o grama" = gram (weight); "a grama" = grass. The (M) annotation marks this as the measurement sense.
reason: Standard BP word for the unit of weight. The gendered-meaning tag is the key learner risk: using the wrong gender shifts the word to "grass". The English gloss alone doesn't cause misuse, but the gender distinction could mislead a learner who ignores the (M) annotation.

example_pt: Eventualmente eu tomo café à tarde, mas não sempre.
example_en: I occasionally have coffee in the afternoon, but not always.
risk_note: False friend: eventualmente means "occasionally/sometimes", NOT "eventually". For "eventually" use "finalmente" or "por fim".
reason: Classic BP false friend. The English gloss "eventually" is the misleading cognate; eventualmente in BP means "occasionally/sometimes". The example confirms the correct BP meaning. Learners will almost certainly misuse this.

example_pt: Vós sois bem-vindos à nossa casa.
example_en: You are welcome to our house.
risk_note: Vós (2nd-person plural) is archaic/obsolete in everyday BP; Brazilians use vocês instead. Mainly found in religious, literary, or EP contexts.
reason: Vós as a 2nd-person plural pronoun is effectively obsolete in Brazilian speech; vocês has fully replaced it. Retaining vós in active BP use risks sounding archaic or EP-influenced. Tags confirm bp-rare.

example_pt: O maciço dos Andes é muito alto.
example_en: The Andes mountain range is very high.
reason: Standard BP geographical term for a mountain massif/range. No learner-safety issue; the example sentence clearly illustrates the geographical sense.

example_pt: Ela se consagrou como a melhor atleta do ano.
example_en: She was recognized as the best athlete of the year.
reason: Standard BP verb; reflexive sense (consagrar-se = to be recognized/established as) is natural and common. Cognate with English "consecrate" but the reflexive social-achievement sense is well-established in BP. No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: Este mapa é muito confuso para mim.
example_en: This map is very confusing for me.
reason: Standard BP adjective used for both "confusing" (causing confusion) and "confused" (feeling confusion). The annotation specifies the "causing confusion" sense here, which is normal and unremarkable. No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: O maestro rege a orquestra no teatro hoje.
example_en: The conductor conducts the orchestra at the theater today.
reason: Standard BP verb used across multiple senses (rule, manage, conduct music). The music/conducting sense in the example is natural and unambiguous. No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: O coral da igreja canta todos os domingos.
example_en: The church choir sings every Sunday.
reason: Standard BP word for a choral group/choir. Cognate with English "choral"; no learner-safety issue. The example confirms the choral-group sense clearly.

example_pt: Meu avô estudou no liceu quando era jovem.
example_en: My grandfather studied at high school when he was young.
risk_note: In Brazil, "colégio" or "escola" is used for high school; "liceu" sounds European/archaic to most Brazilians.
reason: "Liceu" is closely associated with European Portuguese (and French-influenced education systems); in Brazil it survives only in some historical institution names. Everyday BP uses "colégio", "escola secundária", or "ensino médio" instead.

example_pt: Não obstante a chuva, fomos ao parque.
example_en: Notwithstanding the rain, we went to the park.
reason: Used almost exclusively in the fixed phrase 'não obstante'; valid formal/literary BP but low-frequency in everyday speech. No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: Ela colocou a camisola antes de dormir.
example_en: She put on her nightgown before sleeping.
risk_note: In BP, camisola = nightgown. In EP, it means sweater. English "camisole" is unrelated. Don't confuse with EP usage.
reason: Standard BP word for nightgown; tagged false_friend because EP uses camisola for sweater, and English "camisole" is a false cognate. No other risk.

example_pt: Estou confuso com as instruções do exercício.
example_en: I'm confused with the exercise instructions.
reason: Common BP adjective meaning "confused" (state of mind). Cognate with English; no learner-safety issues. The dual gloss "confused/confusing" is a normal adjective ambiguity (e.g., "estou confuso" vs "é confuso") that the example sentence resolves clearly.

example_pt: O elenco do filme é muito talentoso.
example_en: The cast of the film is very talented.
reason: Common, everyday BP word for a cast/troupe of performers. No learner-safety issue; straightforward translation confirmed by example.

example_pt: Meu noivo pediu minha mão em casamento no mês passado.
example_en: My fiancé asked for my hand in marriage last month.
reason: Standard BP noun for fiancé/bridegroom. The annotation 'before wedding' simply disambiguates the sense (fiancé vs. husband). No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: Não obstante a chuva, fomos à praia.
example_en: Notwithstanding the rain, we went to the beach.
reason: Valid BP prepositional phrase but formal/literary; uncommon in everyday speech. Matches annotation and #bp-rare tag. No learner-safety risk.

example_pt: Aquando da reunião, todos estavam presentes.
example_en: At the time of the meeting, everyone was present.
risk_note: Sounds distinctly European Portuguese in Brazil; Brazilians would more naturally say "durante" or "na época de". May sound odd or overly formal in BP.
reason: Aquando is tagged #bp-rare and is strongly associated with EP usage. While a Brazilian might understand it, it is rarely used in natural BP speech or writing; "durante" or "na época de" are preferred.

example_pt: O noivo esperava a noiva no altar da igreja.
example_en: The bridegroom was waiting for the bride at the church altar.
reason: Standard BP word for bridegroom (on wedding day) or fiancé. No learner-safety issue; the annotation clarifies the specific sense in context.

example_pt: O coral do mar é colorido e bonito.
example_en: The sea coral is colorful and beautiful.
reason: Standard BP word for the marine organism/material sense. Cognate with English "coral"; no learner-safety issue. The "choral" sense (choir) shares the same lemma in BP but the annotation and example clearly scope this to the marine/material sense.

example_pt: A casa tem cinco cômodos, incluindo a cozinha.
example_en: The house has five rooms, including the kitchen.
risk_note: BP spelling is "cômodo" (with circumflex), not "cómodo". The display form with acute accent is EP; learners should use the BP spelling.
reason: The word itself is standard BP for "room" (cômodo), but the headword is spelled with the EP accent (cómodo). The example correctly uses the BP spelling "cômodos". Learners must learn the BP spelling with circumflex.

example_pt: O lume aquecia a casa na noite fria.
example_en: The fire warmed the house on the cold night.
risk_note: In Brazil, "lume" is rare and literary/archaic; Brazilians say "fogo" or "chama" instead. The word sounds distinctly European Portuguese.
reason: "Lume" for fire/light is common in EP but rare and literary/archaic in BP. The #bp-rare tag confirms this. A learner using it in everyday Brazilian speech would sound unnatural or EP-influenced.

example_pt: Eles moram nos arredores da cidade.
example_en: They live in the suburbs of the city.
reason: Valid BP but low-frequency; typically used in the plural form 'arredores' (as in the example). No learner safety issue.

example_pt: A resposta do pedido ainda está pendente.
example_en: The response to the request is still pending.
reason: Normal BP adjective meaning "pending/waiting"; cognate with English. No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: O lume da vela ilumina o quarto.
example_en: The light of the candle illuminates the room.
risk_note: More common in EP than BP; Brazilians typically say "luz" (light) or "fogo/chama" (fire/flame). Using "lume" may sound EP or literary.
reason: "Lume" is tagged bp-rare and uncommon; it is the everyday word for "fire/flame" in EP but feels literary or archaic in most of Brazil, where "luz" and "fogo/chama" are preferred. Learners should know the BP alternatives.

example_pt: Moro no arredor da cidade, longe do centro.
example_en: I live in the outskirts of the city, far from downtown.
reason: Valid BP but low-frequency; Brazilians typically say "arredores" (plural) or "periferia/subúrbio". Singular "arredor" is uncommon but not wrong or risky.

example_pt: Meus avós moram em um país longínquo.
example_en: My grandparents live in a far away country.
reason: Valid BP adjective but low-frequency and literary/formal in tone; everyday BP would more commonly use "distante" or "longe". No learner-safety issue; just worth noting the register.

example_pt: O elenco de convidados inclui vários artistas famosos.
example_en: The list of guests includes several famous artists.
risk_note: Primary BP meaning is "cast" (theater/film). "List/index" is a secondary sense. Using elenco for a generic list may sound odd; use lista instead.
reason: Elenco in BP primarily means a cast of performers (teatro/cinema). The "list/enumeration" sense exists but is secondary and less common; learners taught "list" as primary may misapply the word.

example_pt: O rinoceronte tem um corno grande no nariz.
example_en: The rhinoceros has a big horn on its nose.
risk_note: Primary slang meaning in BP: a man whose partner cheats on him (cuckold). The animal "horn" sense is valid but secondary; context usually disambiguates.
reason: In Brazil, 'corno' is overwhelmingly associated with the cuckold insult. The animal/horn sense exists (as in the example) but learners must know the dominant slang meaning to avoid unintended offense.

example_pt: Ele receia perder o emprego.
example_en: He fears losing his job.
reason: Valid BP verb but low-frequency in everyday speech; Brazilians typically prefer 'temer' or 'ter medo de'. No learner-safety issue; just a formal/literary leaning word that is uncommon in casual BP.

example_pt: A indústria farmacêutica desenvolve novos medicamentos.
example_en: The pharmaceutical industry develops new medicines.
reason: Standard BP technical/health adjective; cognate with English "pharmaceutical". No learner-safety issue.

example_pt: Este sofá é muito cómodo para assistir TV.
example_en: This sofa is very comfortable for watching TV.
risk_note: The spelling "cómodo" with an accent is EP orthography. In BP the standard spelling is "cômodo" (with a circumflex). Using the EP form may look foreign in Brazil.
reason: Under the 1990 Orthographic Agreement (in force in BP since 2009), the accent on this word is a circumflex: "cômodo". The acute-accented form "cómodo" is European Portuguese. The adjective sense itself is perfectly normal BP; only the spelling diverges.

example_pt: O farmacêutico explicou como tomar o remédio.
example_en: The pharmacist explained how to take the medicine.
reason: Standard BP noun for pharmacist; common in everyday and health-care contexts. No learner-safety issues. The English gloss lists both "pharmaceutical" (adj sense) and "pharmacist" (noun sense), but the noun sense classified here is unambiguous.

example_pt: Ela leva uma vida casta e simples.
example_en: She leads a chaste and simple life.
reason: Valid BP adjective but low-frequency in everyday speech; used in formal, literary, or religious contexts. Cognate with English 'chaste'; no learner-safety issue.

example_pt: Aquele banana não sabe dirigir.
example_en: That fool doesn't know how to drive.
risk_note: Masculine "o banana" means fool/wimp; the feminine "a banana" is just the fruit. Using the wrong article changes the meaning entirely.
reason: Standard informal BP slang for a spineless/foolish person, but only in the masculine form (o banana). The gender distinction is a real learner trap: wrong article = wrong meaning.

example_pt: O protetor solar é essencial na praia.
example_en: Sunscreen is essential at the beach.
